title: Maitreyi asks for more
hookLine: Yajnavalkya is about to leave home and offers his wife Maitreyi a share of his wealth. she asks for something else
carry: scripture: breathed out by brahman, and the way to know
last: JNANA: THE SALT IN EVERY SIP.

cards: In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the great sage Yajnavalkya decides to leave home for the wandering life. He tells his wife Maitreyi he'll settle his property between her and his other wife, Katyayani.
Maitreyi asks: if this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. You'd live like the rich, but there's no hope of immortality through wealth.
Then what would I do with it? she answers. Tell me what you know. So he does.
The self, he tells her, is what must be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on.

teach.b: Shankara leans on that breath when he reads the Brahma Sutra's third line, which says, in effect: because of being the source of scripture. The key word is yoni, a source, a womb. He reads it two ways and keeps both.

teach.h: SOURCE OF SCRIPTURE, AND THE WAY.
teach.b: First: Brahman is the source of scripture. Texts that light up all things like a lamp, he says, can only come from something all-knowing, as easily as breathing.
Second: scripture is the source, meaning the way, of knowing Brahman. The senses can't reach it, and reasoning alone can't settle it; the Upanishads can.
That's why Hindus call the Veda shruti, what was heard: many hold that no human composed it, and that the seers heard it.

And it's why the Advaita path of jnana follows Yajnavalkya's words to Maitreyi: hear the teaching from a teacher, reflect on it, meditate until it's known. Other Vedanta schools comment on this line in their own ways.
Today we're surrounded by words, endless feeds of them. This tradition holds that a few words, heard well, can open onto what no screen can show.

how: Vedanta schools treat the Upanishads as the means of knowing Brahman; in Advaita, students hear them from a teacher (shravana), reflect on them (manana) and meditate on them (nididhyasana).

o: a chant repeated to earn a good rebirth
the act of copying sacred texts by hand

games.q: Maitreyi and the third line — tap the pairs.
p: Brahman is the source of scripture
scripture is the way to know Brahman

s: Maitreyi took her share of the wealth and let Yajnavalkya go
she asked what use wealth was if it couldn't make her immortal, and asked for his teaching instead.
Shankara reads the third line only one way
he gives two readings, one after the other, and lets both stand.
in the Brihadaranyaka, the Vedas are described as breathed out
like smoke from a fire of damp wood. Shankara leans on that image for his first reading.

games.q: the third line says: because of being the source of scripture. you're Shankara. which reading do you give?
o: Brahman is the source of scripture.
scripture is the source for knowing Brahman.
games.why: he gives both. one says where the texts come from; the other says what they're for.

practice: Choose one line: the self is what must be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on, or a verse your family loves. Hear it once, slowly, out loud or silently. Turn it over for a few breaths: what is it saying?
Then let the words go, and rest in what they point to. If you pray, let the line be your prayer; if you don't, simply rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing. On the third line, Shankara finds two directions: Brahman as the source of scripture, and scripture as the way jnana arrives.

orig.note: Sanskrit: source, womb, place of origin; the key word of Brahma Sutra 1.1.3.

carryVoice: Your line: scripture: breathed out by brahman, and the way to know. Maitreyi asked for more than wealth. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.1–2.4.5 (Yajnavalkya about to leave; the settlement with Katyayani; Maitreyi: would the earth full of wealth make me immortal?; 'tell me what you know'; the self to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on)
Brahma Sutra 1.1.3 (because of being the source of scripture)
Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.3 (two readings: Brahman the source of the Rig Veda and the rest, which illumine all things like a lamp; scripture the means of knowing Brahman)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.10 (as smoke billows from a fire laid with damp fuel, so the Rig Veda and the rest are the breathing out of this great being)
